22670-jack-wright-and-his-electric-stage:
Jack Wright and His Electric Stage, or Leagued Against the James Boys, is a dime novel of the famous boy inventor Jack Wright and his marvelous electric stagecoach. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. The Jack Wright stories, printed in cheap weeklies, pitted the young inventor's machines against the West's most famous outlaws.

In the sample, the hunters plan an ambush at a curve where timber, brush, and rocks jut close to the road. There the train must slacken speed, and the ground will hide their movements from the sheriff's view. Wheels, wires, and gunplay mix freely in this kind of tale. The book is pure period pulp: swift, improbable, and proud of it, built for boys with a nickel and an afternoon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beja:
Beja is a Portuguese diocese, suffragan of Evora, created in 1770 with 175,000 Catholics, 115 parishes, and 197 churches. Its city, capital of Baixo Alemtejo, is thought to be Rome's Pax Julia, still ringed by partly medieval-restored Roman walls. Affonso Henriques took it from the Moors in 1162, and it stands on a high hill amid fertile valleys of cereals, oil, and wine.

Its castle, built by King Dom Diniz, is a square mass 120 feet high, Portugal's finest surviving medieval architecture. From its top the whole Alemtejo and the Cintra mountains can be seen, and its walls bear hieroglyphics. An early episcopal city, it lost that dignity under the Moors, and its cathedral is now too modernized to date. The city holds about 8,000 people and ranks richest in Roman remains after Evora.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-:
Francisco de Rioja, born at Seville in 1583 and dead at Madrid in 1659, was a Spanish poet and canon of Seville cathedral who also served the Supreme Inquisition. His poems, Quintana judged, were the first attempts at descriptive poetry in Castilian, original in style, beautifully thought, refined in taste, and versified in harmony with their themes. Menendez y Pelayo ranked his odes to summer, tranquillity, constancy, riches, and poverty just after the lyrics of Fray Luis de Leon among Castilian moral odes.

Two famous poems long given to Rioja are not his. The ode on the ruins of Italy belongs to Rodrigo Caro, and the moral epistle probably to Francisco de Andrada. Yet stripped of those gems he remains highly esteemed by Spanish scholars. His best edition is Barrera's of 1867, with additions in 1872, and his finest poems appear in Rivadeneira's library of Spanish authors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-par:
Francisco Pareja, probably born at Aunon in the diocese of Toledo and dead in Mexico on 25 January 1628. He was a Franciscan missionary who published the first books in an Indian language within the present United States. Sent to Florida with eleven other Franciscans, he arrived at St. Augustine in 1593 or early 1594 and laboured among the peoples of the peninsula, notably at San Juan on the coast. He became guardian of the monastery of the Immaculate Conception at St. Augustine, later styled custos before the custody became a province in 1613.

Joining the province of the Holy Gospel in Mexico, he gave the Timuquanan language its first printed literature. It began with a catechism in Spanish and Timuquanan in 1612, a brief exposition of Christian doctrine the same year, a confessional in both languages in 1613. A grammar of Timuquanan followed in 1614, another catechism in 1617, and a catechism and examination for communicants in 1627.

maruja:
Bret Harte set his novel Maruja on the high road to San Jose. Dawn breaks over wheat and oat fields in the first scene. A coyote and a young tramp cross the plain, half a mile apart.

Man and beast share a lazy, stray look in Harte's close prose. The tramp turns off the road to dodge the dogs of a farm. He rests in a hollow of wild clover, with bread crusts and time to waste. Harte lingers on light, dust, and scent as the day warms. The slow start builds the old California world the title figure rules.
